title: Analyzers
jupyter: python3

An analyzer records something during a run that the results don't keep, without changing the model. Most quantities don't need one: every state and transition of a declared disease has a result, ratios and outcomes are declared with the model (see [Results](running_results.qmd)), and results by age or any other group come from [stratifying](models_stratification.qmd) the model. An analyzer is for the rest: something about individual agents (their ages when infected, who infected whom), or a quantity worked out from several modules at once.

## When an analyzer runs

An analyzer runs at the start (time point 0) and then at the end of each step, after the step's results have been recorded. In the analyzer, `sim.ti` (or `self.ti` in a class) is the time point at the end of the step, where the step's results go. A declared disease dates each infection at the end of the step in which it happened, in its state `ti_I`, so the people infected during this step are those with `ti_I == ti`. An analyzer that acts every few steps (`if self.ti % 7 == 0`, at the end of each week) also acts at time point 0, before anything has happened, unless it skips it (`if self.ti == 0: return`).

## A function as an analyzer

The simplest analyzer is a function of the sim, given in `analyzers=`. This one records the mean age of the people infected in each step, which is a common measure for measles (where vaccination of children raises it). It needs individual ages, so the sim runs as agents:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
infection = S >> I @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.001)

ages = []
def age_at_infection(sim):
    new = sim.diseases.measles.ti_I == sim.ti # People infected during this step
    ages.append(sim.people.age[new].mean() if new.any() else np.nan)

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), analyzers=age_at_infection, verbose=0)
sim.run()
print('Mean age at infection, by step:', np.round(ages[1:9], 1))
```

Here people mix at random, so the mean age at infection is close to the mean age of the population; with a contact matrix in which children mix most, it would be lower.

A function is quick to write, but what it records lives outside the sim: it is not plotted or exported with the results, and when the sim is run in another process (by `ss.parallel()`), the list in this process stays empty. For anything kept, use a class.

## An analyzer as a class

An analyzer written as a class (a subclass of `ss.Analyzer`) declares results of its own, which are then stored, plotted, and exported with the sim's other results. This one records the mean age at infection, and the new infections among children and adults, as one result with a column for each:

```{python}
class AgeAtInfection(ss.Analyzer):
    """ The mean age of the people infected in each step, and the number of them who are children and adults """
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('mean_age', label='Mean age at infection', scale=False), # An average, so not scaled by the people each agent stands for
            ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'], label='New infections'),
        )

    def step(self):
        new = self.sim.diseases.measles.ti_I == self.ti
        if new.any():
            age = self.sim.people.age
            self.results.mean_age[self.ti] = age[new].mean()
            self.results.new_infections[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(new & (age < 15)), np.count_nonzero(new & (age >= 15))]

sim = ss.Sim(measles, n_agents=10_000, stop=ss.days(30), dt=ss.days(0.25), analyzers=AgeAtInfection(), verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.results.ageatinfection.new_infections.plot()
```

The analyzer's results are under its name in lower case, `sim.results.ageatinfection`. A result with columns has each as a result of its own (`res.new_infections.children`), and each is a column of `sim.to_df()`:

```{python}
sim.to_df().columns.tolist()
```

A result declared with `scale=True` (the default) is a count, which is multiplied by the number of people each agent stands for when the run ends; an average or a share takes `scale=False`.

## The infection log

The infection log records each infection: when it happened, who was infected, and, where there is a network, by whom. It needs agents and a contact network, since otherwise nobody is the source of a particular infection. Give `analyzers='infection_log'`:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
flu = ss.Disease(S >> I @ 0.05*I, I >> R @ ss.days(8), init_prev=0.002, name='flu')

sim = ss.Sim(flu, networks=ss.RandomNet(n_contacts=8), n_agents=5_000, stop=ss.days(100), analyzers='infection_log', verbose=0)
sim.run()
log = sim.analyzers.infection_log.log
df = log.to_df()
df.tail()
```

Each row is one infection: the time (`t`), the infected agent (`target`), and the agent who infected them (`source`, which is −1 for the people infected at the start). The log also plots who infected whom over time, and `log.to_graph()` gives the chains of transmission as a NetworkX graph:

```{python}
sim.analyzers.infection_log.plot()
```

`animate()` shows the same infections as they happen, one frame per time point: each agent infected is a dot on a grid, colored by when it was infected. It draws each frame in turn, so run it in a Python session rather than a notebook:

```{python}
#| eval: false
sim.analyzers.infection_log.animate(framerate=20)
```

From the log, the generation interval (the time from a person's infection to the infection of each person they infect) is the time of each infection minus the time its source was infected:

```{python}
infected_at = df.set_index('target').t        # When each agent was infected
df['generation'] = df.t - df.source.map(infected_at)
print('Mean generation interval:', round(df.generation.mean(), 1), 'days')
```

If a person's contacts all stayed susceptible, the mean would be the mean infectious period, 8 days. It is shorter because they don't: on a network, a person's contacts are soon infected by others or immune, so people infect fewer of them late in their infectious period.

A disease written as code can add data to each infection, such as the variant (`log.add_entries(uids, sources, time, variant=variants)`), or to each agent's latest infection later on, such as a diagnosis (`log.add_data(uids, diagnosed=True)`). See [Modules written as code](models_code.qmd).

## Analyzers in a compartmental run

An analyzer can be given to a model that runs as compartments, as any module written as code can that keeps nothing for each person. There, it sees the number of people in each compartment, not individuals: `sim.diseases.measles.I.n` is the number infectious. The run then goes a step at a time, so it is slower; for a quantity that can be worked out from the results after the run, such as the effective reproduction number R0 × S/N, compute it from the results instead.

## Pitfalls

- **An analyzer must not change the model.** To change something during a run, use an [intervention](interventions_products.qmd).
- **Results kept outside the sim are lost** when the sim runs in another process (`ss.parallel()`); declare results in a class.
- **Counts of agents are scaled; averages are not.** Declare an average or a share with `scale=False`.
- **Check whether a result already exists.** Stratifying the model gives results by age or any other group, under every solver, with no analyzer.
